decisions.question: e-5573

source.question: e-5573
source.value:
Since the set $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} 
= \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}_1}\mathbf{x} + \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbf{x}.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1\}$ and $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_2\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{2\cdot 1+3\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=1[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{2\cdot (-2)+3\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 1}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+(-\frac{1}{2})[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

decisions.question: e-7173

source.question: e-7173
source.value:
Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3.$ 
And, since the set $\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by   

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} = \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\,\mathbf{x} + \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{w}}\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}\}$ and $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{w}\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{13\cdot 2+(-2)\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot (-1)}{{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}v=\frac{3}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{13\cdot 5+(-2)\cdot (-3)+(-1)\cdot 1}{{5}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}w=2[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

source.value:
Since the set $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} 
= \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}_1}\mathbf{x} + \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbf{x}.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1\}$ and $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_2\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{3\cdot 1+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{1}=\frac{4}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{3\cdot 1+2\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =\frac{4}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(3-2)}^{2}+{(2-2)}^{2}+{(1-2)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

decisions.question: e-7309

source.question: e-7309
source.value:
Since the set $\{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} 
= \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{x} + \textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{w}}\mathbf{x}.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}\}$ and $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{w}\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{v}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot v}{v\cdot v}v=\frac{\sqrt{10}\cdot 0+3\cdot 1+1\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}v=2[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {\text{proj}}_{w}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot w}{w\cdot w}w=\frac{\sqrt{10}\cdot 0+3\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1}{{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}w=(-1)[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{v}\,x+{\text{proj}}_{w}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

The acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $\mathbf{x}$ and $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}$ or any other non-zero vector that is parallel to $\textrm{proj}_S \mathbf{x}.$ So, computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x\cdot {\text{proj}}_{S}\,x}{‖x‖\,‖{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x‖} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{10}\cdot 0+3\cdot 3+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{(\sqrt{10})}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{10}{\sqrt{20}\,\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{10}{10\,\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta = \arccos\left( \dfrac{{\sqrt2}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4},
$$

which is already an acute angle.
